title: On stochastic realism and CP bias in diffractive dissociations
abstract: CP bias in proton--antiproton diffractive dissociation can be viewed from several philosophical perspectives, notably stochastic realism and stochastic epistemicism. When combined with the presumption of temporal symmetry, stochastic realism suggests that the laws of physics allow the possibility of thermodynamic antisystems, although whether antisystemic characteristics can be physically realised in nature remains an open question.   Here, this bias is interpreted as apparent, indicating significant non-unitary contributions and a distinction from fundamental CP violations arising from unitary Hamiltonian dynamics. Such apparent effects may arise from intrinsic stochasticity, from environmental interactions, or from interference between the two. This work investigates the relevant mechanisms and determines conditions for creating, transmitting, or screening a CP bias.   In the environmental branch, an equilibrated radiation bath may transmit a CP bias from matter-dominated surroundings, although causality constraints may limit this possibility. In the intrinsic branch, the observed bias is consistent with subleading antisystemic effects required by CPT invariance. Further experiments are needed to distinguish between these mechanisms.
summary: This work investigates the apparent nature of CP violation observed in particle collisions by modeling the system as an open quantum system. It develops a framework using stochastic realism to distinguish between fundamental symmetry breaking and effects arising from environmental interactions or intrinsic randomness. The paper concludes that while time asymmetry is mathematically permitted, further experiments are needed to pinpoint the exact physical source of any measured bias.
main_problem: The paper interprets the observed CP bias in proton–antiproton diffractive dissociation by analyzing how symmetries are affected when quantum evolution is non-unitary.
main_result: The observed CP bias is argued to be apparent, stemming from non-unitary effects (intrinsic stochasticity or environmental interactions) rather than fundamental violations of CP symmetry arising from unitary dynamics.
method: The analysis combines philosophical frameworks (stochastic realism vs. epistemicism) with rigorous quantum mechanical treatments of open systems using Redfield equations and stochastic differential equations.
model_or_system: The primary system is proton–antiproton diffractive dissociation, analyzed through the lens of open quantum systems interacting with environmental baths or undergoing intrinsic stochastic evolution.
key_observables: Statistically significant CP bias in cross-section ratios and dephasing rates; comparison between fundamental (unitary) vs. apparent (non-unitary) symmetry violations.
important_parameters: The distinction between unitary Hamiltonian dynamics and non-unitary contributions from environmental or intrinsic stochasticity.
main_assumptions: It assumes that the observed bias can be modeled by considering both environmental coupling (radiation bath) and inherent system randomness, while also utilizing concepts like CPT invariance constraints.
figures_summary: Figure 1 contrasts stochastic epistemicism with stochastic realism; Figure 2 schematically illustrates dual temporal boundary conditions for time-asymmetry analysis.
paper_structure: The paper moves from interpreting the observed CP bias using philosophical lenses, to analyzing general time asymmetry in stochastic systems (dual boundaries), and finally applying these concepts to open quantum system dynamics via Redfield equations to determine symmetry preservation under decoherence.
why_interesting: It provides a deep theoretical link between fundamental symmetries (CPT) and emergent phenomena in complex, non-equilibrium systems, which is crucial for understanding measurement processes in AMO physics.
